chapter.title: The one equation

cards.body:
Every balance sheet ever printed adds up, down to the cent. Not because accountants are careful, but because it cannot do otherwise.

Think of one house on one day. The house and everything in it is what you **own**. The mortgage and the unpaid bills are what you owe. Whatever is left is yours. A balance sheet is that photo, taken of a company.
cards.simpler:
Every balance sheet adds up to the cent. That is not because accountants are careful. It is because the sheet cannot do anything else.

Picture one house on one day. The house and everything inside it is what you **own**. The mortgage and the unpaid bills are what you owe. Whatever is left belongs to you. A balance sheet is that same photo, but taken of a company.

cards.prompt: Priya's flat would sell for 300,000. Her mortgage is 220,000. Over coffee a friend asks: so how much of that flat is actually yours?

whyNot.a: That's what she owns, not what's hers: the bank still has a claim on 220,000 of it.
whyNot.c: That's own and owe added together, but the mortgage is a claim against the flat, so it comes off, not on.

cards.reteach: Start with the whole house. Take away everything that must be paid back to someone else. What stays is the owner's share. 300,000 minus 220,000 leaves 80,000.

cards.title: Three totals, three words
cards.body:
A balance sheet has three totals, and they are the three parts of the house. *Assets* are what the company owns: cash in the bank, boxes in the warehouse, the building, the vans. *Liabilities* are what it owes: loans, unpaid supplier bills, tax due. *Equity* is what is left for the owners once every debt is paid.

The sheet has two sides. One lists assets. The other lists liabilities, then equity underneath. **Assets equal liabilities plus equity**, every time.

You'd think the owners' share is a number someone decides. It isn't. It is what falls out when you subtract.
cards.simpler:
A balance sheet has three totals. Assets are what the company owns: cash, stock in the warehouse, the building, the vans. Liabilities are what it owes: loans, unpaid bills, tax due. Equity is what is left for the owners after every debt is paid.

One side lists assets. The other lists liabilities, then equity. **Assets equal liabilities plus equity**, every single time. The owners' share is not a number someone picks. It is whatever is left when you subtract.

cards.title: Marta's oven
cards.body:
Marta opens a bakery. She puts in 40,000 of her own savings and borrows 60,000 from the bank. She buys an oven for 50,000 and keeps 50,000 as cash.

Assets: oven 50,000 plus cash 50,000, total 100,000. Liabilities: the loan, 60,000. Equity: 40,000. Nobody wrote 40,000 down as equity; it is the **only number that could sit there**. The bank's share of the oven is not painted on the oven. It is written on the sheet.
cards.simpler:
Marta opens a bakery. She puts in 40,000 of her own savings and borrows 60,000 from the bank. She buys an oven for 50,000 and keeps 50,000 in cash.

What she owns: oven 50,000 plus cash 50,000, so 100,000. What she owes: the loan, 60,000. Her share: 40,000. Nobody chose it. It is the **only number that could sit there**. The bank's share of the oven is not painted on the oven. It lives on the sheet.

cards.prompt: A printout shows total assets of 500 million and total liabilities of 320 million. Coffee has landed on the equity line. What was under the stain?

options.text: Can't tell without knowing the profit

whyNot.a: That's assets plus liabilities: equity is what remains after the debts, so you subtract.
whyNot.c: That's the income statement talking, not the balance sheet: equity is fixed by the other two totals on this one day.

cards.reteach: Equity is never a mystery number. It is what you own minus what you owe. 500 minus 320 is 180, coffee or no coffee.

cards.title: Why it can never be off
cards.body:
Why does it always balance? Because the two sides are not two piles of money. They are **one pile, counted twice**: once by what it is, once by where it came from.

Every euro of assets arrived through one of two doors. Someone lent it, so it shows up as a liability. Or the owners put it in, or earned it and kept it, so it shows up as equity. There is no third door.

So when a sheet doesn't balance, the company isn't poorer. Someone typed a number wrong. A balanced sheet proves the arithmetic, not the health. That part comes later.
cards.simpler:
Why does it always balance? The two sides are not two piles of money. They are **one pile, counted twice**: once by what it is, once by where it came from.

Each euro used one of two doors. Lent by someone? It shows as a debt. Put in or earned by the owners? It shows as their share. There is no third door.

If a sheet does not balance, someone typed a wrong number. Balancing proves the sums, not the health.

cards.body: Tom spots 'total assets: 2 billion' at the top of a sheet and tells his flatmate the company is worth 2 billion. He never looked across to the other side, where 1.9 billion of loans sat waiting. **The house price is not what the homeowner has.** If someone quotes you assets alone, ask what the mortgage is.
cards.simpler: Tom sees 'total assets: 2 billion' at the top of a sheet. He tells his flatmate the company is worth 2 billion. He never looked at the other side, where 1.9 billion of loans was waiting. **The house price is not what the homeowner has.** If someone quotes you assets alone, ask what the mortgage is.

cards.prompt: A company takes out a new 10 million loan and the cash lands in its account the same day. What happens on the balance sheet?

options.text: Assets up 10 million, equity up 10 million
Assets up 10 million, liabilities up 10 million
Assets up 10 million, nothing else, so the sheet stops balancing

whyNot.a: That's what happens when the owners put money in, not the bank: a loan is a claim, so it lands in liabilities.
whyNot.c: A real event can't unbalance the sheet: the cash came from somewhere, and that somewhere is the bank's claim.

cards.reteach: The cash is new, so assets grow. But the cash came through the lender's door, so liabilities grow by the same amount. Both sides move together; the owners' share hasn't changed.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
A balance sheet lists what a company owns, what it owes, and what's left for the owners, and the first always equals the other two added together. It balances because every asset was paid for by either a lender or an owner, so there is **no third place for money to come from**.

Tomorrow: why a balance sheet is a photo, not a film.
cards.simpler:
A balance sheet lists three things. What a company owns, what it owes, and what is left for the owners. The first always equals the other two added together. It balances because every asset was paid for by a lender or by an owner. There is **no third place for money to come from**.

Tomorrow: why a balance sheet is a photo, not a film.

cards.body: Search the name of any listed company you know plus 'annual report balance sheet'. Find total assets, total liabilities and total equity. Add the last two. Check they match the first.
cards.simpler: Pick any listed company you know. A listed company is one whose shares trade on a stock exchange. Search its name plus 'annual report balance sheet'. Find three lines: total assets, total liabilities and total equity. Add the last two together. **Check they match the first.** They should, to the cent.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now find the three totals on any balance sheet and show that what it owns equals what it owes plus what belongs to the owners.
